blocks.body:
If $f'(a) \ne 0$ for a function of one variable with continuous derivative, then $f$ is strictly monotonic near $a$, so it has an inverse there, and $(f^{-1})'(f(a)) = 1/f'(a)$. The inverse function theorem is the same statement for maps $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$: if the derivative matrix at a point is invertible, then near that point the map can be undone, and the inverse is as smooth as the map.

Its companion, the implicit function theorem, says when an equation $F(x,y) = 0$ can be solved for some variables as smooth functions of the others, even if no formula exists. Together they justify change of variables, Lagrange multipliers, and the idea that a nondegenerate level set is a smooth curve or surface.

blocks.title: Linearisation, and what can go wrong
blocks.body:
Near a point $a$, a $C^1$ map is approximately affine: $f(a+h) \approx f(a) + Df(a)\,h$, where $Df(a)$ is the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives ([[partial-derivatives]]). If the matrix $Df(a)$ is invertible, the affine approximation is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (see [[linear-maps]]), and the theorem says the true map inherits this, but only near $a$.

Polar coordinates show both the power and the limit of the statement. Let $f(r,\theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$. Its Jacobian is

$$Df(r,\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det Df = r.$$

So $f$ has a smooth local inverse around every point with $r > 0$. It has no global inverse on $\{r > 0\}$, because $f(r,\theta) = f(r,\theta + 2\pi)$: invertibility of the derivative everywhere gives local injectivity everywhere, not global injectivity. At $r = 0$ the determinant vanishes, and indeed the whole line $r = 0$ is squashed to a single point.

A one-variable table shows why continuity of the derivative matters. The map $f(x) = x + 2x^2\sin(1/x)$ (with $f(0) = 0$) has $f'(0) = 1$, but $f'(x) = 1 + 4x\sin(1/x) - 2\cos(1/x)$ equals $-1$ at every $x = 1/(2\pi k)$ and $3$ at every $x = 1/((2k+1)\pi)$. So $f$ goes up and down infinitely often near $0$ and is not injective on any interval around $0$. The theorem needs $f \in C^1$.

blocks.title: C¹ maps and diffeomorphisms
blocks.body:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open. A map $f : U \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is $C^1$ if all partial derivatives $\partial f_i/\partial x_j$ exist and are continuous on $U$; then $f$ is differentiable with derivative the $m \times n$ Jacobian matrix $Df(x)$. A $C^1$ bijection $f : V \to W$ between open sets whose inverse is also $C^1$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.

We use the operator norm $\|A\| = \sup_{|h| = 1}|Ah|$ for matrices, and the fact that if $A$ is invertible and $\|B - A\|\,\|A^{-1}\| < 1$ then $B$ is invertible too (invertible matrices form an open set).

blocks.title: Inverse function theorem
blocks.body:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $f : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ a $C^1$ map, and $a \in U$ a point where $Df(a)$ is invertible. Then there are open sets $V \ni a$ and $W \ni f(a)$ such that $f$ maps $V$ bijectively onto $W$, the inverse $g : W \to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg\big(f(x)\big) = Df(x)^{-1} \qquad (x \in V).$$

If $f$ is $C^k$ for some $k \ge 1$, so is $g$.

blocks.title: Proof via contractions
blocks.body:
The idea is to solve $f(x) = y$ by a fixed-point iteration and use the [[contraction-mapping|contraction mapping principle]].

Set $A = Df(a)$ and choose $\lambda > 0$ with $2\lambda\|A^{-1}\| = 1$. Since $Df$ is continuous, there is an open ball $V$ around $a$ in $U$ on which $\|Df(x) - A\| < \lambda$. For each $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ define

$$\varphi_y(x) = x + A^{-1}\big(y - f(x)\big).$$

Then $f(x) = y$ exactly when $\varphi_y(x) = x$. Also $D\varphi_y(x) = A^{-1}\big(A - Df(x)\big)$, so $\|D\varphi_y(x)\| < \|A^{-1}\|\lambda = \tfrac12$ on $V$. Since $V$ is convex, the mean value inequality gives $|\varphi_y(x_1) - \varphi_y(x_2)| \le \tfrac12|x_1 - x_2|$ for $x_1, x_2 \in V$.

Injectivity. A contraction has at most one fixed point, so for each $y$ there is at most one $x \in V$ with $f(x) = y$. Let $W = f(V)$; then $f : V \to W$ is a bijection.

$W$ is open. Let $y_0 = f(x_0)$ with $x_0 \in V$, pick $r > 0$ with the closed ball $\overline{B} = \overline{B}(x_0, r) \subset V$, and let $|y - y_0| < \lambda r$. For $x \in \overline{B}$,

$$|\varphi_y(x) - x_0| \le |\varphi_y(x) - \varphi_y(x_0)| + |\varphi_y(x_0) - x_0| \le \tfrac{r}{2} + \|A^{-1}\|\,|y - y_0| < \tfrac r2 + \tfrac r2 = r.$$

So $\varphi_y$ is a contraction of the complete metric space $\overline{B}$ into itself, and has a fixed point there: $y \in f(\overline{B}) \subseteq W$. Thus $B(y_0, \lambda r) \subseteq W$.

$g$ is differentiable. Fix $y \in W$, $x = g(y)$, and for small $k$ put $h = g(y + k) - x$. Then $\varphi_y(x + h) - \varphi_y(x) = h - A^{-1}k$, whose length is at most $|h|/2$; hence $|A^{-1}k| \ge |h|/2$ and $|h| \le 2\|A^{-1}\|\,|k| = |k|/\lambda$. In particular $h \to 0$ as $k \to 0$. Since $\|Df(x) - A\|\,\|A^{-1}\| < \tfrac12$, the matrix $Df(x)$ is invertible; call its inverse $T$. Now

$$g(y+k) - g(y) - Tk = h - Tk = -T\big(f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h\big),$$

so

$$\frac{|g(y+k) - g(y) - Tk|}{|k|} \le \frac{\|T\|}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|}{|h|} \to 0 \quad (k \to 0)$$

(when $h = 0$ the left side is $0$). So $Dg(y) = T = Df(g(y))^{-1}$. This is continuous in $y$, being the composition of the continuous maps $g$, $Df$ and matrix inversion; so $g$ is $C^1$. If $f$ is $C^k$, the formula $Dg = (Df)^{-1}\circ g$ and induction on $k$ show $g$ is $C^k$.

blocks.title: Implicit function theorem
blocks.body:
Write points of $\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ as $(x,y)$ with $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Let $F$ be a $C^1$ map from an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ with $F(a,b) = 0$, and suppose the $m \times m$ matrix $D_yF(a,b) = \big(\partial F_i/\partial y_j\big)$ is invertible. Then there are open sets $U \ni a$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $V \ni b$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and a $C^1$ map $g : U \to V$ such that for $(x,y) \in U \times V$,

$$F(x,y) = 0 \iff y = g(x),$$

and $Dg(x) = -\big(D_yF(x,g(x))\big)^{-1}D_xF(x,g(x))$.

Define $\Phi(x,y) = (x, F(x,y))$, a $C^1$ map from an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$. Its Jacobian at $(a,b)$ is the block matrix

$$D\Phi(a,b) = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & 0\\ D_xF(a,b) & D_yF(a,b)\end{pmatrix},$$

whose determinant is $\det D_yF(a,b) \ne 0$. By the inverse function theorem $\Phi$ maps an open set around $(a,b)$, which we may shrink to a product $U_0 \times V$, diffeomorphically onto an open set $W \ni (a, 0)$. Because $\Phi$ does not change the first coordinate, its inverse has the form $\Phi^{-1}(x,z) = (x, h(x,z))$ with $h$ of class $C^1$. Let $U = \{x \in U_0 : (x, 0) \in W\}$, an open set containing $a$, and put $g(x) = h(x, 0)$.

For $x \in U$ and $y \in V$: $F(x,y) = 0$ means $\Phi(x,y) = (x,0)$, which (since $\Phi$ is injective on $U_0 \times V$) means $(x,y) = \Phi^{-1}(x,0) = (x, g(x))$. Finally, differentiating $F(x, g(x)) = 0$ with the chain rule gives $D_xF + D_yF\,Dg = 0$, which is the formula for $Dg$; $D_yF(x,g(x))$ is invertible near $a$ by continuity, after shrinking $U$ if necessary.

blocks.title: Level sets and solving equations
blocks.body:
For the circle $F(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 = 0$, $\partial F/\partial y = 2y$. At every point with $y \ne 0$ the theorem lets us write the circle locally as a graph $y = g(x)$ (here $g(x) = \pm\sqrt{1-x^2}$), with $g'(x) = -F_x/F_y = -x/y$. At $(\pm1, 0)$ it fails, and genuinely so: near $(1,0)$ each $x < 1$ has two nearby $y$'s and each $x > 1$ has none. There one solves for $x$ instead, since $F_x = 2x \ne 0$.

The general picture: if $F : \mathbb{R}^{n+m} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is $C^1$ and $DF$ has full rank $m$ at every point of the level set $F = 0$, then near each point some choice of $m$ variables can be solved for in terms of the other $n$, so the level set is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function of $n$ variables: an $n$-dimensional surface. Such level sets are called regular, and this is the standard way of producing [[smooth-manifolds]]. It is also what makes [[lagrange-multipliers]] work: on such a surface, a constrained extremum of $f$ forces $\nabla f$ to be a combination of the rows of $DF$.

Two refinements for later. The constant rank theorem says that if $Df$ has constant rank $k$ near a point, then in suitable local coordinates $f$ looks like $(x_1,\dots,x_n) \mapsto (x_1,\dots,x_k,0,\dots,0)$. And there are infinite-dimensional versions on Banach spaces with the same proof, used to show that solutions of nonlinear differential equations depend smoothly on parameters.

blocks.title: Inverting polar coordinates
blocks.body: Show that polar coordinates have a $C^1$ local inverse near $(r,\theta) = (2, \pi/3)$, and compute the derivative of the inverse at $(x,y) = (1, \sqrt3)$ in two ways.
blocks.solution:
At $(2,\pi/3)$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}1/2 & -\sqrt3\\ \sqrt3/2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $2 = r \ne 0$, so the theorem applies. By the formula $Dg = (Df)^{-1}$,

$$Dg(1,\sqrt3) = \frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & \sqrt3\\ -\sqrt3/2 & 1/2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1/2 & \sqrt3/2\\ -\sqrt3/4 & 1/4\end{pmatrix}.$$

Directly: near this point the inverse is $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, $\theta = \arctan(y/x)$. Then $r_x = x/r = 1/2$, $r_y = y/r = \sqrt3/2$, $\theta_x = -y/r^2 = -\sqrt3/4$ and $\theta_y = x/r^2 = 1/4$, matching the matrix above.

blocks.title: An equation with no closed-form solution
blocks.body: Show that $xe^y + y = 1$ defines $y$ as a $C^1$ function $g(x)$ near $(1,0)$, and find $g'(1)$ and $g''(1)$.
blocks.solution:
Let $F(x,y) = xe^y + y - 1$. Then $F(1,0) = 0$ and $F_y = xe^y + 1$, which is $2 \ne 0$ at $(1,0)$, so the implicit function theorem gives $g$ with $g(1) = 0$ (and $g$ is $C^\infty$ since $F$ is).

Differentiate the identity $xe^{g} + g = 1$:

$$e^{g} + xe^{g}g' + g' = 0.$$

At $x = 1$, $g = 0$: $1 + 2g'(1) = 0$, so $g'(1) = -1/2$. (This is $-F_x/F_y = -1/2$.) Differentiate again:

$$2e^{g}g' + xe^{g}(g')^2 + xe^{g}g'' + g'' = 0.$$

At $x = 1$: $-1 + \tfrac14 + 2g''(1) = 0$, so $g''(1) = 3/8$. Near $x = 1$, then, $g(x) \approx -\tfrac12(x-1) + \tfrac{3}{16}(x-1)^2$.

blocks.title: Roots depend smoothly on coefficients
blocks.body: Let $$p(x,y,z) = (x+y+z,\; x^2+y^2+z^2,\; x^3+y^3+z^3)$$. Show that $p$ is locally invertible near any point with $x, y, z$ distinct, and not near any point with two coordinates equal. Interpret this for the roots of a cubic.
blocks.solution:
The Jacobian is

$$Dp = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 1\\ 2x & 2y & 2z\\ 3x^2 & 3y^2 & 3z^2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det Dp = 6\,(y-x)(z-x)(z-y),$$

a multiple of the Vandermonde determinant. So if $x, y, z$ are distinct, $Dp$ is invertible and $p$ has a $C^1$ (indeed $C^\infty$) local inverse.

If two coordinates are equal, say $x = y$, then for small $t \ne 0$ the points $(x+t, x-t, z)$ and $(x-t, x+t, z)$ are distinct, arbitrarily close to $(x,x,z)$, and have the same image (because $p$ is symmetric). So $p$ is not injective on any neighbourhood: local invertibility genuinely fails, not just the hypothesis.

By Newton's identities the power sums determine the elementary symmetric functions and conversely, so the coefficients of $t^3 - e_1t^2 + e_2t - e_3 = (t-x)(t-y)(t-z)$ are smooth functions of the power sums and vice versa. The conclusion: near a cubic with three distinct real roots, the roots, labelled continuously, are smooth functions of the coefficients. At a double root this breaks down, as $t^2 = \varepsilon$ shows: its roots $\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ are not differentiable in $\varepsilon$ at $0$.

blocks.body:
- The theorem is local. $f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2, 2xy)$, which is $z \mapsto z^2$ in complex notation, has $\det Df = 4(x^2+y^2) \ne 0$ away from the origin, yet it is two-to-one on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$.
- Invertible derivative is sufficient, not necessary, for an inverse: $x \mapsto x^3$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$ with $f'(0) = 0$. What fails is the smoothness of the inverse: $x^{1/3}$ is not differentiable at $0$.
- Differentiability alone is not enough; you need $C^1$ (see $x + 2x^2\sin(1/x)$ above).
- In the implicit function theorem, the invertible block must be the derivative with respect to the variables you are solving for. Checking $\det D_xF$ instead tells you about solving for $x$.

The proof is an application of the [[contraction-mapping]] principle, and the same fixed-point scheme is a simplified Newton's method ([[root-finding]]). The implicit function theorem underlies [[lagrange-multipliers]], the change of variables formula for [[multiple-integrals]], and the definition of curves and surfaces as regular level sets; on [[smooth-manifolds]] the inverse function theorem is the tool that makes charts, immersions and submersions work, and it reappears for [[differential-forms]] and [[lie-groups]]. In [[holomorphic|complex analysis]] the analogous statement is that a holomorphic function with $f'(a) \ne 0$ is locally biholomorphic, the starting point for [[conformal-maps]].

1. For $f(x,y) = (e^x\cos y, e^x\sin y)$, compute $\det Df$, show that $f$ is locally invertible everywhere, and explain why it is not globally injective.
2. Show that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + \sin(xyz) = 1$ defines $z$ as a $C^1$ function of $(x,y)$ near $(0,0,1)$, and compute $\partial z/\partial x$ and $\partial z/\partial y$ at $(0,0)$.
3. Prove that if $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is $C^1$ and $Df(x)$ is invertible for every $x$, then $f(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is open.
4. Near which points of the curve $y^2 = x^3$ can the curve be written as $y = g(x)$ with $g$ of class $C^1$? As $x = h(y)$? What happens at the origin?

sources.ref: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.)
